# Do We Always Need the Simplicity Bias? Looking for Optimal Inductive Biases in the Wild

**Teney, Jiang, Gogianu & Abbasnejad — "Do We Always Need the Simplicity Bias? Looking for Optimal Inductive Biases in the Wild"** · arXiv:2503.10065 (v1) · serialisation: the native arXiv HTML, converted with page marks against the arXiv PDF (task-008, 2026-08).

**An external work; the abstract is given.** The subject of the paper is the limits of the simplicity bias and the meta-learning of activation functions for particular tasks. Grokking is one of four areas of application; what the corpus values here is the tenfold acceleration by spline activations and their learned sine-likeness. Set aside by the triage of task-021 (2026-08-26). No work of the corpus cites it yet. The introduction and the quoted paragraphs are translated lazily, as quotations appear (decision D2-b). The original — [`original/`](original/2503.10065.do-we-always-need-the-simplicity-bias-looking-for-optimal-inductive-biases-in-the-wild.md); the analysis of the claims is the neighbouring `…claims.txt`.

# Abstract

*"Neural architectures tend to fit their data with relatively simple functions. This “simplicity bias” is widely regarded as key to their success. This paper explores the limits of this principle. Building on recent findings that the simplicity bias stems from ReLU activations Teney et al. 2024b, we introduce a method to meta-learn new activation functions and inductive biases better suited to specific tasks."*
